Annotations 71 LITTLE BUNNY 5 “The master’s job is not to produce a copy. The master’s job is to produce a practitioner.” — Little Bunny LITTLE BUNNY 7 — I — What Gets Passed Down Most of what gets passed down between a master and an apprentice is not the technique. The technique is available. You can read about it, watch it, study it from the outside. What cannot be transmitted through observation alone is

the decision-making architecture — the moment-by-moment calibration of when to speak, when to hold, when to advance, and when to absorb. This book is about that transmission. It is also, necessarily, about failure — because the apprentice always fails before they succeed, and the quality of that failure is the most diagnostic information the master has access to. A clean failure means the apprentice understood the principle and missed the execution. A messy failure means the principle itself has not yet arrived. The conversations in this volume are drawn from a documented mentorship relationship that spanned four years. The master had been practicing the Framework, under various names and in various professional contexts, for nearly two decades. The apprentice came in with intelligence, competitive instincts, and a working theory of people that was approximately seventy percent correct. Seventy percent is dangerous. It is close enough to feel like mastery. It is far enough from mastery to produce catastrophic misreads at exactly the moments that matter. This book tracks the process of closing that gap. LITTLE BUNNY 25 — III — Score 1: The Alignment Test The first scored exchange the master ran on the apprentice was not labeled as a test. It arrived as a question during a routine debrief. The apprentice did not know he was being scored until

the annotation was delivered three days later. This was intentional: the test environment must be real or the score is contaminated. MASTER 7 "Tell me what you think happened in that conversation yesterday. The one with the client." PLT NOTE: Score 7: Open invitation but with directionality. ‘What you think happened’ vs ‘what happened’ — he’s already signaling he wants interpretation, not recitation. APPRENTICE 4 "She seemed defensive from the jump. I think she didn’t want to be in the meeting and was doing us a favor by showing up." PLT NOTE: Score 4: Perceptive but passive. ‘Seemed’ and ‘think’ are hedge words. He’s reading the room but hasn’t committed to the read. The master will push here. MASTER 8 "What did she say in the first two minutes that made you think that." PLT NOTE: Score 8: No question mark. He’s asking for evidence, not impression. This is the Framework’s first discipline: close the gap between observation and assertion. APPRENTICE 8 "She didn’t make eye contact when she introduced herself. She said ‘sure, let’s do this’ instead of anything more engaged. And she checked her phone once before we even sat down." PLT NOTE: Score 8: Evidence-based and specific. He has the data. The problem was he didn’t lead with this — he led with the conclusion. Order matters

in the Framework. Data before interpretation. MASTER 9 "Good. Now say what you said at the start — but start with those three things." PLT NOTE: Score 9: He’s teaching structure, not content. The apprentice had the right material in the wrong order. This is a masterclass move: instead of correcting the error, he makes the apprentice self-correct through resequencing. LITTLE BUNNY 43 — V — The Transfer There is a moment in every apprenticeship when the doctrine stops being the master’s and starts being the apprentice’s. This does not happen during a ceremony. It happens during a live exchange, under pressure, when the apprentice makes a decision that the master would have made — not because they were told to make it, but because they have internalized the logic well enough to arrive there independently. The transfer is recognizable because the master stops coaching and starts watching. The apprentice’s score in the exchange below was 9. The master gave it without hesitation. CLIENT (3RD PARTY) 4 "I’ve heard good things about the Framework but I’m not sure it applies to my situation. I’m in financial services. Very different from what you work on." PLT NOTE: Score 4 (client): This is pre-emptive dismissal through industry differentiation. The Framework scores this as defensive positioning — he’s trying to exit before he’s

fully entered. APPRENTICE 9 "What specifically is different? Because the Framework doesn’t address industry — it addresses how people talk to each other under pressure. That happens in financial services every day." PLT NOTE: Score 9: He asked a clarifying question that was also a reframe. He didn’t defend the Framework — he redefined its jurisdiction. The client is now on the hook to specify the difference, which he cannot do without engaging the Framework’s actual premise. LITTLE BUNNY 71 — VIII — Annotations The apprenticeship documented in this volume produced, over four years, an independent practitioner. The final scored exchanges — Chapter VII — were conducted without the master present. The scores were applied retroactively, from transcripts. They held. When a student’s scores in solo execution match their scores in supervised execution, the transfer is complete. The diagnostic question for any master is not ‘has the apprentice learned the technique?’ It is ‘has the apprentice learned why the technique works?’ The first produces imitation. The second produces judgment. Judgment is what you need when the situation is unfamiliar. The Framework is always operating in unfamiliar situations.
